packet.headline_seed: Illicit deeds have just gotten a new Halloween video game banned in Australia – and it’s not because of the violence

Academics – and a former director of Australia’s Classification Board – say Halloween: The Game’s ban due to ‘incentivised drug use’ highlights an incoherent set of standards Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast Halloween’s Michael Myers is one of film’s most feared boogeymen, responsible for some of the most brutal on-screen deaths in horror cinema. US video game developer Illfonic looked to reproduce those terrors in its upcoming title Halloween: The Game, with gruesome killings a major focus of the gameplay: for instance, you can stomp another player’s head through a toilet seat, or fry their brain by throwing them through a television screen.

But Australians will not be able to play Halloween: The Game, because it has been refused classification by the Classification Board, which means it is banned from sale within the country. And it’s not because of the violence or murders. In the game, players can smoke marijuana to see the location of Michael Myers in order to avoid being killed – a use of drugs that Australia’s Classification Board has deemed a “gameplay advantage”. Under the Guidelines for the Classification of Computer Games 2023, video games are refused classification if they contain “illicit or proscribed drug use related to incentives or rewards”.

“Halloween: The Game contains illicit drug use that is linked to an incentive or reward, in that use of the drug provides a gameplay advantage to the player. It is on this basis that the game has been refused classification, as required under the Code and Guidelines,” the board wrote in a recent statement. In the wake of the decision, Illfonic’s social media accounts have been flooded with comments from irate Australians. An FoI officer said the Classification Board had received more than 500 complaints in relation to Halloween: The Game. The uproar has resurfaced longstanding grievances about how games are classified in Australia compared to film and television, and the inability for adults to access games widely available in other parts of the world.

[Lähde: The Guardian World | URL: https://www.theguardian.com/games/2026/aug/24/michael-myers-halloween-video-game-banned-in-australia-drugs]
Academics – and a former director of Australia’s Classification Board – say Halloween: The Game’s ban due to ‘incentivised drug use’ highlights an incoherent set of standards

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Halloween’s Michael Myers is one of film’s most feared boogeymen, responsible for some of the most brutal on-screen deaths in horror cinema. US video game developer Illfonic looked to reproduce those terrors in its upcoming title Halloween: The Game, with gruesome killings a major focus of the gameplay: for instance, you can stomp another player’s head through a toilet seat, or fry their brain by throwing them through a television screen.

But Australians will not be able to play Halloween: The Game, because it has been refused classification by the Classification Board, which means it is banned from sale within the country. And it’s not because of the violence or murders.

In the game, players can smoke marijuana to see the location of Michael Myers in order to avoid being killed – a use of drugs that Australia’s Classification Board has deemed a “gameplay advantage”. Under the Guidelines for the Classification of Computer Games 2023, video games are refused classification if they contain “illicit or proscribed drug use related to incentives or rewards”.

“Halloween: The Game contains illicit drug use that is linked to an incentive or reward, in that use of the drug provides a gameplay advantage to the player. It is on this basis that the game has been refused classification, as required under the Code and Guidelines,” the board wrote in a recent statement.

In the wake of the decision, Illfonic’s social media accounts have been flooded with comments from irate Australians. An FoI officer said the Classification Board had received more than 500 complaints in relation to Halloween: The Game.

The uproar has resurfaced longstanding grievances about how games are classified in Australia compared to film and television, and the inability for adults to access games widely available in other parts of the world.

Claire Henry, associate professor in screen at Flinders University and an Australian Research Council Decra fellow, says the board enforced the guidelines correctly but the controversy around the decision highlights “a mismatch between the community standards and the classification standards”.

The decision on Halloween: The Game follows several high-profile cases that have seen games such as State of Decay, Wasteland 3

payload.title: Halloween-peli sai Australiassa myyntikiellon kannabiksesta saatavan peliedun vuoksi
payload.summary: Australia epäsi Halloween: The Gamen luokituksen, koska marihuanan polttaminen auttaa pelaajaa paikantamaan Michael Myersin. Päätös on tuonut luokittelulautakunnalle yli 500 valitusta.
payload.content:
Yhdysvaltalaisen pelinkehittäjän Illfonicin tuleva Halloween: The Game on jäänyt Australiassa ilman virallista luokitusta, mikä estää sen myynnin maassa. Ratkaisun syynä ei ole pelin raaka väkivalta vaan kannabiksen käyttö: pelihahmo saa siitä konkreettisen edun nähdessään tappaja Michael Myersin sijainnin ja voi yrittää välttää surmatuksi joutumisen.

Kauhuelokuvista tuttu Michael Myers on pelin keskeinen uhka. Myers tunnetaan elokuvissa pelottavana hahmona ja poikkeuksellisen raaoista valkokankaalla tehdyistä surmista. Illfonic on pyrkinyt tuomaan elokuvien kauhun pelimuotoon, ja julmat tappamistavat ovat merkittävä osa pelaamista. Pelaaja voi esimerkiksi painaa toisen hahmon pään wc-istuimen läpi tai surmata tämän heittämällä hänet television kuvaruudun läpi. Luokitteluratkaisu ei kuitenkaan perustunut näihin kohtauksiin.

## Huumeista saatu pelietu ratkaisi

Australian vuoden 2023 tietokonepelien luokitteluohjeiden mukaan peli on jätettävä luokittelematta, jos siinä esiintyvä laiton tai kielletty huumeidenkäyttö liittyy kannustimeen tai palkintoon. Halloween-pelissä hahmo voi polttaa marihuanaa nähdäkseen Michael Myersin sijainnin. Luokittelulautakunta katsoi tämän pelaajalle annettavaksi pelilliseksi eduksi.

Lautakunta ilmoitti lausunnossaan, että huumeiden käyttö on pelissä sidottu kannustimeen tai palkintoon juuri sen tarjoaman peliedun vuoksi. Sen mukaan luokitus oli siksi evättävä voimassa olevan säännöstön ja ohjeiden perusteella. Australiassa luokittelematta jätettyä peliä ei saa myydä, joten päätös merkitsee käytännössä myyntikieltoa.

## Päätös synnytti yli 500 valitusta

Päätös on herättänyt voimakkaan vastareaktion. Illfonicin sosiaalisen median tileille on tullut runsaasti vihaisten australialaisten kommentteja. Luokittelulautakunnan tiedonsaantiasioista vastaavan virkamiehen mukaan lautakunta on lisäksi vastaanottanut Halloween: The Gameen liittyen yli 500 valitusta.

Kohu on kasvanut yksittäistä peliä laajemmaksi kiistaksi Australian luokittelusäännöistä. Se on nostanut uudelleen esiin pitkään jatkuneen arvostelun siitä, että pelejä kohdellaan eri tavoin kuin elokuvia ja televisiota. Tutkijat ja luokittelulautakunnan entinen johtaja ovat pitäneet ratkaisussa näkyviä standardeja epäjohdonmukaisina. Arvosteluun liittyy myös se, etteivät aikuiset voi Australiassa hankkia pelejä, jotka ovat saatavilla muualla maailmassa.

Luokittelulautakunta on saanut päätöksestä yli 500 valitusta.

Se on nostanut uudelleen esiin pitkään jatkuneen arvostelun siitä, että pelejä kohdellaan eri tavoin kuin elokuvia ja televisiota. Tutkijat ja luokittelulautakunnan entinen johtaja ovat pitäneet ratkaisussa näkyviä standardeja epäjohdonmukaisina. Arvosteluun liittyy myös se, etteivät aikuiset voi Australiassa hankkia pelejä, jotka ovat saatavilla muualla maailmassa.

Academics – and a former director of Australia’s Classification Board – say Halloween: The Game’s ban due to ‘incentivised drug use’ highlights an incoherent set of standards Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast Halloween’s Michael Myers is one of film’s most feared boogeymen, responsible for some of the most brutal on-screen deaths in horror cinema. US video game developer Illfonic looked to reproduce those terrors in its upcoming title Halloween: The Game, with gruesome killings a major focus of the gameplay: for instance, you can stomp another player’s head through a toilet seat, or fry their brain by throwing them through a television screen.

But Australians will not be able to play Halloween: The Game, because it has been refused classification by the Classification Board, which means it is banned from sale within the country. And it’s not because of the violence or murders. In the game, players can smoke marijuana to see the location of Michael Myers in order to avoid being killed – a use of drugs that Australia’s Classification Board has deemed a “gameplay advantage”. Under the Guidelines for the Classification of Computer Games 2023, video games are refused classification if they contain “illicit or proscribed drug use related to incentives or rewards”.

“Halloween: The Game contains illicit drug use that is linked to an incentive or reward, in that use of the drug provides a gameplay advantage to the player. It is on this basis that the game has been refused classification, as required under the Code and Guidelines,” the board wrote in a recent statement. In the wake of the decision, Illfonic’s social media accounts have been flooded with comments from irate Australians. An FoI officer said the Classification Board had received more than 500 complaints in relation to Halloween: The Game. The uproar has resurfaced longstanding grievances about how games are classified in Australia compared to film and television, and the inability for adults to access games widely available in other parts of the world.
